analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to let every worker earn up to seven paid sick days a year.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate in February 2026 with 35 cosponsors — every one a Democrat or independent — and referred to committee, where no vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The Healthy Families Act would require nearly every employer in the country to let workers earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours (about seven workdays) a year. The time could be used for a worker's own illness or doctor visits, to care for a child, spouse, parent, or domestic partner, or to deal with domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking. Employers that already offer at least as much paid leave for the same purposes would not have to change anything. The bill was referred to the Senate committee that handles labor law and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who have no paid sick time today, especially part-time, low-wage, and service workers, gain a guaranteed bank of paid days off for illness and family care. Caregivers, domestic violence survivors, and workers who currently show up sick to avoid losing pay also gain. Public health gains too, since fewer people work while contagious.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers without paid sick time, especially low-wage and part-time

how_it_helps.text: Requires employers to provide at least 1 hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours a year, paid at the worker's regular rate.

Lets workers use the time for their own physical or mental illness, medical diagnosis or preventive care, care for family members including domestic partners, and absences related to domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking.
Makes it unlawful for an employer to fire, retaliate against, or penalize a worker for using the time, including counting it against no-fault attendance policies.
Gives workers a direct right to sue for lost wages and reinstatement, with attorney's fees paid by a violating employer, and lets the Labor Department investigate and enforce.

analysis.who_pays: Employers bear the cost of paying wages for sick days their workers did not previously get, plus new recordkeeping, notice-posting, and compliance duties. Small businesses and low-margin industries with many hourly workers face the largest new payroll costs, and some of the cost may be passed to consumers or offset in hiring.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, especially small and hourly-heavy businesses

drawbacks.text: The mandate requires employers to pay wages for up to 56 hours per employee per year that many did not budget for, hitting small businesses and low-margin sectors like food service and retail hardest.
Employers must keep compliance records, post notices, and can be fined up to $100 per willful posting violation, adding administrative burden on top of the payroll cost.

A worker who takes more than 3 consecutive sick days can be required to provide a doctor's certification, which is a real hurdle for people without a regular doctor or health insurance; the bill acknowledges this by requiring special rules for the uninsured.
Unused sick time does not have to be paid out when a worker leaves the job, so the benefit has no cash value at separation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a genuine tradeoff rather than a one-sided bill. The benefit is concrete for the large share of American workers who get no paid sick time today: seven guaranteed paid days a year to be sick or care for family, with real penalties for retaliation. The cost is also concrete: it is a new federal payroll mandate, and businesses that would carry it, particularly small ones, argue it raises labor costs and may slow hiring. Exempting employers that already offer equivalent leave, preserving stronger state and local laws, and capping the requirement at 56 hours moderate the burden. How it nets out depends on how much of the cost is absorbed by employers versus passed to workers and consumers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate committee that handles labor law in February 2026, and it has sat there since with no hearing, no markup, and no vote scheduled; the Republican majority that runs the committee includes not a single cosponsor.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) introduced the Healthy Families Act in the Senate on February 12, 2026, with 30 original cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced; the action history shows no further steps since.
It has 35 cosponsors — 34 of the 45 Senate Democrats and 1 of the 2 independents — and no Republican has signed on.

The bill would require 1 hour of paid sick time per 30 hours worked, capped at 56 hours a year, usable for a worker's own illness or medical care, care for family members, and situations involving domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking.
Employers that already provide an equivalent amount of paid leave for the same purposes are not required to add anything, and stronger state or local paid sick leave laws are preserved.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far the bill has only been referred to committee, so no one has won or lost yet. If it stalls in committee, the employers who would have paid for the new benefit come out ahead, and the many workers who currently get no paid sick time are no better off than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who would have paid the new benefit

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont; bill's lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Healthy Families Act on February 12, 2026.

for.name: 34 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it one of the most broadly supported Democratic bills in the Senate.

against.name: 55 of 55 Senate Republicans
against.role: Senate majority; controls the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: None of the 55 Republican senators has cosponsored the bill, and the committee their majority controls has taken no action on it beyond receiving the referral.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and allied business groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed earlier versions of this same paid-sick-leave mandate, arguing it imposes payroll and compliance costs on employers.

sides.party_line_note: Support is entirely Democratic and independent — 34 of 45 Senate Democrats, 1 of 2 independents, and 0 of 55 Republicans — and the bill has not yet reached a floor vote where positions could be tested further.

industries.industry: Low-wage service employers (restaurants, retail, hospitality, call centers)
industries.note: These industries employ the largest share of workers without any paid sick time, so they would face the largest new payroll costs — paid wages for up to 56 hours per worker per year — plus scheduling and recordkeeping duties. Their interest in avoiding the mandate runs against the workers the bill covers.

The bill covers employers with as few as one employee, so small firms must track hours earned, post notices, and pay for sick days they did not previously offer. Firms that already provide equivalent paid leave are exempt, which softens the hit for some.

industries.industry: Employers with generous existing paid leave policies
industries.note: The bill ratifies their current policies as sufficient and requires nothing more, effectively locking in paid leave as a standard benefit rather than letting it be scaled back. These employers gain a level playing field against competitors that would otherwise skip the benefit.

analysis.trajectory: With the bill parked in a committee run by the majority party, no Republican cosponsor, and roughly ten months left in the Congress, the realistic path is the usual one for a bill at this stage: no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the session ends. It would need to be reintroduced in a future Congress with broader support to advance.
